name: Freya Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No problem. I'm in the farm office, so if you hear pigs, that's why.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm unit manager at Marsh Lane, which is owned by a farming company. We've a finishing unit, about 2,000 pigs from weaning to sale, plus 400 acres of wheat and oilseed rape. I'm in at half six, walk every pen, and look at every pig, because the feeding and ventilation are already automatic but they can't tell you a pig's off-colour. Then it's medicine records, the vet's visit on Tuesdays, and the harvest plan with the arable lads, Pete and Callum.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's home like, and how are you fixed for money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sami, my husband, is a mechanic at the machinery dealer in town, mostly tractors and combines. Our twins are 27, Noor's in accounts and Adam drives for a delivery firm. We gave Noor most of what we'd saved for her house deposit last year, so we're down to about three weeks of money. I don't regret it, but it's made me jumpy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was overhyped, like most things. I'd say it at the Tuesday vet visit and we'd have a laugh. I'm not big online, maybe a comment on the pig farmers' group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine by me. We've already got automatic feeders and climate control, and they're handy. A bit more of the same and nothing radical suits me well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to check a ration or draft a note to the area manager. The main thing I'd do is rebuild the savings after Noor's deposit, about a hundred a month if we're careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the automatic feeders can't tell when a pig's off-colour. How do you tell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The way they stand, mostly. A pig that's off will hang back from the feeder with its ears down, or its tail's not curled. I've caught pneumonia two days before the monitors would because a pen sounded wrong at half six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to rebuild the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The takeaways on Friday, that's Sami's treat, he'll moan. And the gym membership I haven't used since June. The pigs keep me fit enough.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped like most things, and have a laugh about it at the vet visit. Maybe a comment on the pig farmers' online group.
S0.think: I think it's fine by me, since we already have automatic feeders and climate control that help. More of the same with nothing radical suits me.
S0.do: Carries on as unit manager, using AI now and then to check rations or draft notes. Rebuilds savings after helping her daughter with a deposit, about a hundred a month, cutting takeaways and an unused gym membership.
S0.quote: I've caught pneumonia two days before the monitors would because a pen sounded wrong at half six.
S0.fieldNote: She already works with a lot of automation and sees it as normal. Her low savings came from helping her daughter, a choice she stands by but which makes her cautious. Her stockmanship is sensory and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and we'll adapt like we did with the automatic feeders. I'd say the company should train people properly, not just drop new kit on us. Sensible stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be alright. The company would bring in camera systems that spot sick pigs and maybe a robot for washing pens, which is the worst job on the unit. Somebody still has to manage it, and I'd make sure that's me. And Sami would be busier than ever fixing it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the company trial it at one of their other units first, then put my hand up to run it here. I'd do whatever training they offered. I'd keep putting money aside, because I'm not daft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a knot about the lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which lads?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete and Callum on the arable side. Self-driving tractors and spraying drones would hit them harder than anything hits me. Callum's got a baby on the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd make sure it's you running it. How?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By being the one who knows it best, same as with the feeders in 2015. I wasn't the first to like them, but once they were in, I read the manual cover to cover. Area managers notice who reads the manual.

S1.say: I'd say it's change and we'll adapt like we did with the automatic feeders. The company should train people properly, not just drop new kit on us.
S1.think: I think I'd be alright, because someone still has to manage camera systems and pen-washing robots, and I'd make sure that's me. My husband would be busier than ever fixing it all.
S1.do: Lets the company trial new kit at another unit first, then volunteers to run it locally and takes all the training offered. Keeps saving each month as a precaution.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, with a knot of worry for the arable workers.
S1.quote: Area managers notice who reads the manual.
S1.fieldNote: Her household has a hedge: her husband's mechanic work could grow with more machines. She waits for proof elsewhere, then commits fully, as she did with feeders in 2015. Her concern goes to younger colleagues on the arable side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the government needs to catch up, quickly. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it. People need time and some support, that's just common sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is where I lose. If AI can watch the pigs better than me and robots can wash and move them, the company doesn't need a unit manager on site, just someone on a screen two hundred miles away. And if robots fix robots, Sami's job goes too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut hard, straight away, no car upgrade, no holidays, everything into savings. I'd ask Sami's dealer if they'd take me on in parts or admin, anything to get a foot in the machine side. And I'd sit down with the twins and tell them we may need help, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's the word. Both of us at once is what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with more warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No time to get the savings back after Noor's deposit, that's the bit that stings. With five years I'd have rebuilt something. With two, we're starting from almost nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you regret the deposit, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Noor's got a house, and if everything goes, at least one of us does. That's a strange comfort, but it is one.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and the government needs to catch up quickly. People need time and some support, and that's just common sense.
S2.think: I think this is where I lose, because the company could watch pigs from a screen far away and robots could fix robots too. Both our jobs could go at once.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard straight away and puts everything into savings. Asks her husband's dealer about a parts or admin job and tells her grown children they may need help.
S2.feel: Alarmed, mostly by the idea of both incomes going at once.
S2.quote: Noor's got a house, and if everything goes, at least one of us does.
S2.fieldNote: The household's hedge disappears here, which is what pushes her to alarm. Two years leaves no time to rebuild savings spent on her daughter's deposit. She still frames the deposit as a good decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so let's plan. Companies and government should agree on training for people my age, not just the young ones. I'd say it at work and to anyone at the dealer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to 63. I think I'd have a role for three or four of those years, running the new kit, and then it gets dicey. But that's three or four years of savings I didn't have in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the bigger units do in year one, then go on whatever course the company runs on the new monitoring systems. I'd also do a short course with Sami on servicing farm robots, so between us we've got both sides covered. And save, hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can manage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Both of you learning the robot side. Is that a plan or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both. Sami's been fixing GPS kit for ten years, so it's a real plan for him. For me it's a hope with a course attached.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Callum, with five years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get his drone licence now, while the company will pay for it. He'll grumble. He grumbled about the feeders too.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to plan, so companies and government should agree on training for people my age, not just the young. I'd say it at work and at the dealer.
S3.think: I think I'd have three or four years running the new kit before it gets dicey. That's three or four years of savings I wouldn't have in the fast scenario.
S3.do: Watches bigger units for a year, then takes the company's course on new monitoring systems. Does a short robot servicing course with her husband and saves hard.
S3.quote: For me it's a hope with a course attached.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her follow her usual pattern of watching first and then learning. She plans as a couple, pairing her skills with her husband's. She was honest that her part of the plan is less certain than his.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, so nobody can say they weren't warned. I'd say companies should start training now and the government should look after people near retirement. Middle-of-the-road, that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me ten years is mostly fine. I'd retire at 66 or so, and by then it'll be someone else's problem. The worry is just whether we've enough to retire on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a few years and see which systems actually work before learning them, like always. I'd keep working at Marsh Lane and save steadily, aiming for a year's cushion by 65. And I'd make sure the twins aren't relying on us, which they aren't, thank goodness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, mostly about the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you work past 66 if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe part-time, helping new managers learn how to read a pig. That's not something a camera gets from a manual. But I'd want to choose it, not need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked a lot about the twins. What would you tell them in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take ten years seriously, don't wait till year eight. I'd tell Adam especially, because delivery driving's going to be one of the first. He'd laugh, but I'd say it anyway.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, so nobody can say they weren't warned. Companies should start training now and the government should look after people near retirement.
S4.think: I think ten years is mostly fine for me, since I'd retire at about 66. The worry is just whether we'll have enough to retire on.
S4.do: Waits a few years to see which systems work before learning them, keeps working at Marsh Lane and saves steadily toward a year's cushion by 65. Warns her son early about driving jobs.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly about her pension.
S4.quote: I'd want to choose it, not need it.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her worry shrinks to retirement money. She keeps her habit of letting others prove the technology first. Her concern shifts to her son's driving job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both of us could lose work at once. What would help is proper notice and paid training for older workers, and some sort of bridge to the pension for people who've done thirty years and can't start over.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what farming's for. It's not just pigs out the door. It's knowing when something's wrong before the numbers say so. I hope someone keeps that.

headlineQuote: It's knowing when something's wrong before the numbers say so.
portrait: Freya Ibrahim is 58 and manages a 2,000-pig finishing unit and 400 acres of arable for a farming company. She already works with automatic feeders and uses AI now and then, and she adopts new kit once it's proven elsewhere, then masters it. Her savings are down to a few weeks after helping her daughter buy a house. Pragmatic and middle-of-the-road, she is calm in the slower scenarios, partly because her mechanic husband's work could grow, but alarmed by AGI in two years, when both their jobs could go at once.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because both she and her husband could lose their work at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Proper notice and paid training for older workers, and a bridge to the pension for people who've worked thirty years and can't start over.
